When you type "www.example.com" into your browser, you're initiating a process called DNS resolution. DNS, or Domain Name System, is like a phonebook for the internet. It translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses, which are the numerical addresses that computers use to communicate with each other. Your browser needs to know the IP address of the server hosting the "www.example.com" website to fetch the webpage.

The first step in DNS resolution is a cache miss. Your computer or your Internet Service Provider (ISP) might have a DNS resolver that caches recently resolved domain names to speed up future lookups. If the resolver doesn't have the IP address for "www.example.com" in its cache, it will start a recursive query.

The recursive resolver starts by querying a root server. Root servers are like the first stop in a phonebook lookup. They don't know the exact IP address of "www.example.com," but they can tell the resolver which top-level domain (TLD) server to ask next. For "www.example.com," the TLD is ".com," so the resolver queries a .com server.

The .com server then directs the resolver to an authoritative name server for "example.com." An authoritative name server is the final authority for a domain name. It holds the actual IP address of "www.example.com" and responds to the resolver with this information. The resolver then returns the IP address to your browser, which can now connect to the server and start fetching the webpage.

If the IP address is in the cache, the process is much faster. The TTL, or Time To Live, is a value in seconds that indicates how long the IP address should be considered valid before the resolver checks again. If the TTL is high, the cache can be used for a longer time, reducing the number of DNS lookups.

DNS resolution and fetching the webpage are two distinct processes. DNS resolution is about finding the IP address of the server, while fetching the webpage involves downloading the HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and other resources from that server. Once the browser has the IP address, it can establish a connection to the server and request the webpage. The server then sends the requested content, which the browser interprets and displays to you.
